prompt: A building has one staff network served by 12 access points. How does a phone tell those 12 radios apart?
hint: One name, many radios.

choices.text: By the SSID, which each AP numbers differently
choices.why: The SSID is the network's name and is identical on all 12.

choices.text: By the BSSID, the MAC address of each radio
choices.why: Right. One SSID, and one BSSID per radio per network.

choices.text: By the channel, since no two APs share one
choices.why: Channels are reused across a building; lesson 7 plans exactly that.

choices.text: By the IP address each AP hands out
choices.why: Addresses come from DHCP on the VLAN, after association, and say nothing about the radio.

prompt: An office hides its SSID "for security". What does that change for a laptop configured to join it?
hint: A client has to name a network it cannot hear.

choices.text: Nothing, since the name is in its settings
choices.why: Because it cannot hear the name, it has to ask for it, by name, everywhere.

choices.text: It encrypts its probe requests
choices.why: Probe requests are sent before any key exists and are never encrypted.

choices.text: It calls the network's name out wherever it goes
choices.why: Right. The hidden name leaks from every device that knows it, in public.

choices.text: It stops roaming between access points
choices.why: It still roams; some devices just do it less gracefully.

prompt: A company runs 3 SSIDs on 10 dual-band access points, every SSID on both bands. How many BSSIDs does it have?
hint: One per network, per radio, per AP.

prompt: In WPA2-Personal, what is fed into PBKDF2 alongside the passphrase to make the PMK?
hint: The second line of psk.py's output changes one thing.

choices.text: The AP's MAC address
choices.why: MAC addresses go into the PTK, in the handshake, not into the PMK.

choices.text: A random number picked by the AP
choices.why: Then the PMK would differ every time; in WPA2 it is fixed for a given passphrase and network.

choices.text: The SSID, as the salt
choices.why: Right. IEEE and IEEE-2 gave unrelated keys from the same passphrase.

choices.text: The date the network was created
choices.why: Nothing time-dependent goes in; the test vector is the same in every year.

prompt: In the four-way handshake, how does the client show the AP that it holds the right PMK?
hint: Something computed from the key, not the key.

choices.text: It sends the PMK in message 2, encrypted with the ANonce
choices.why: The PMK never crosses the air, encrypted or not.

choices.text: Its message 2 carries a MIC made with a key derived from the PMK
choices.why: Right. A wrong PMK gives a wrong MIC, and the AP rejects it.

choices.text: It repeats the passphrase's hash back to the AP
choices.why: That hash is the PMK itself, which is exactly what is never sent.

choices.text: The AP checks the client's MAC against a list
choices.why: A MAC list proves nothing; addresses are sent in clear and randomised.

prompt: Put the messages of the four-way handshake in order.
hint: The AP speaks first, and the group key comes from the AP.
items: Client to AP: SNonce and a MIC
AP to client: the GTK, encrypted, and a MIC
Client to AP: acknowledgement and a MIC
trap: The client can only compute the PTK after it has the ANonce, so the AP's nonce comes first.

prompt: A café's WPA2-Personal passphrase is printed on every table. A customer who knows it records another customer joining. What does the recording give them?
hint: Everything else that goes into the PTK is public.

choices.text: A PTK of no use, since each client's is unique
choices.why: The PTK is unique, but it is computed from the shared PMK plus values sent in clear.

choices.text: That customer's traffic, decrypted
choices.why: Right. With the PMK, both nonces and both addresses, the PTK follows. WPA2-Personal keeps out strangers, not people who know the passphrase.

choices.text: The passphrase, which they already had
choices.why: True but beside the point: the risk is to the other customer's traffic.

choices.text: The other customer's session cookie, but only over HTTP
choices.why: Decrypting the Wi-Fi layer exposes whatever runs over it; HTTPS inside stays protected, which is a different claim.

prompt: Why does a recording of a WPA3-Personal (SAE) join not let anybody test passphrase guesses offline?
hint: What else, besides the password, goes into the values on the air?

choices.text: The frames are encrypted with the passphrase
choices.why: Encrypting with the passphrase would give a guesser exactly something to test against.

choices.text: SAE uses a longer PBKDF2
choices.why: SAE does not hash the passphrase into the PMK at all.

choices.text: The values depend on secrets each side picked and kept
choices.why: Right. Without those secrets a recording has nothing to check a guess against, so every guess needs a live exchange.

choices.text: WPA3 hides the SSID from the recording
choices.why: The SSID is still in the beacons, and hiding it would not help anyway.

prompt: Which of these does WPA3-Personal give that WPA2-Personal does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the rows of the table.

choices.text: Forward secrecy
choices.why: Right. A password learnt later does not open earlier recordings.

choices.text: Required protected management frames
choices.why: Right. Optional in WPA2, required in WPA3.

choices.text: Removing one person without changing the password for everybody
choices.why: The password is still shared; that takes 802.1X.

choices.text: Resistance to offline guessing from a recorded join
choices.why: Right. Each guess needs a live SAE exchange.

choices.text: A different cipher for the data frames
choices.why: WPA3-Personal still encrypts data with AES-CCMP after the same four-way handshake.

prompt: A network runs WPA3 transition mode so that three old barcode scanners keep working. What is the passphrase exposed to?
hint: One passphrase, two ways in.

choices.text: Offline guessing from any recorded WPA2 join
choices.why: Right. The WPA2 half keeps WPA2's weakness, whatever the WPA3 clients do; a separate SSID for the scanners removes it.

choices.text: Nothing extra, since SAE protects it
choices.why: SAE protects the joins that use SAE; the scanners' joins are WPA2.

choices.text: The scanners' own sessions, not the passphrase
choices.why: A recording of a scanner joining is enough to test guesses against the shared passphrase.

choices.text: Disclosure in the beacons of the 6 GHz band
choices.why: Beacons never carry the passphrase, and 6 GHz does not allow transition mode at all.

prompt: The amendment that added protected management frames to 802.11, so that a forged disconnection is ignored, is 802.11___.
hint: One letter.

prompt: Match each 802.1X role to the device that plays it.
hint: Who asks, who relays, who decides.

prompt: Before the RADIUS server has answered, what traffic does the AP let through from a newly associated client?
hint: The port is closed to all but one thing.

choices.text: DHCP and DNS, so the client can find the server
choices.why: The client never talks to the server directly; the AP relays EAP for it.

choices.text: Everything, rate-limited until the verdict
choices.why: A port that passed traffic before the verdict would make the verdict decorative.

choices.text: HTTP, for the sign-in page
choices.why: That describes a captive portal, which is not 802.1X.

choices.text: EAP, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. No DHCP, no DNS, no data until the server says yes.

prompt: A company uses PEAP. Its laptops are set to accept whatever certificate the RADIUS server presents. What is the risk?
hint: Where does the TLS tunnel lead?

choices.text: None, because the password travels inside TLS
choices.why: TLS to an unchecked party protects the password on its way to that party.

choices.text: A network with the same SSID receives the login exchange
choices.why: Right. Checking the server certificate is what makes the tunnel lead to your own server; push that setting to every managed device.

choices.text: The laptops fail to join after the certificate is renewed
choices.why: A client that accepts everything keeps joining after a renewal; that is the trouble.

choices.text: The AP learns each user's password
choices.why: The AP relays EAP and never sees the password, checked or not.

prompt: An employee leaves a company that uses WPA3-Enterprise. What has to change so that their laptop cannot join?
hint: Each person has their own credentials.

choices.text: The shared passphrase on the laptops
choices.why: There is no shared passphrase in 802.1X; that is the point of it.

choices.text: The SSID, so the old profile no longer matches
choices.why: Renaming the network breaks everybody's profile and stops nobody with valid credentials.

choices.text: Their account, disabled on the directory RADIUS checks
choices.why: Right. One change, and the next authentication fails.

choices.text: The RADIUS shared secret on each AP
choices.why: That secret is between the APs and the server; the employee never knew it.

prompt: A new guest SSID with its own passphrase is bridged to the same VLAN as the staff. What can a visitor on it reach?
hint: The passphrase decides who gets on; the VLAN decides where they land.

choices.text: The internet, since the passphrase is different
choices.why: A different passphrase changes who gets on, not where they land.

choices.text: The office LAN, like any staff laptop
choices.why: Right. Same VLAN, same subnet, same reach: separation needs its own VLAN and a firewall.

choices.text: A captive portal first, then the internet
choices.why: There is no portal in this design, and a portal separates nothing anyway.

choices.text: Other visitors, but no staff machines
choices.why: Visitors and staff share one broadcast domain here.

prompt: Match each guest-network measure to what it prevents.
hint: One tool per layer.

pairs.right: Sharing a broadcast domain with the staff

prompt: A hotel wants its guest Wi-Fi to need no password and still keep one guest from reading another's traffic over the air. Which option fits?
hint: Encryption without a shared secret.

choices.text: An open network with a captive portal
choices.why: The portal encrypts nothing; every frame is readable in range.

choices.text: WPA2-Personal with the passphrase on the key card
choices.why: That is a password, and every guest who knows it and records a join reads that guest's traffic.

choices.text: Enhanced Open (OWE)
choices.why: Right. Each client gets its own key from an unauthenticated exchange, with no password to type.

choices.text: A hidden SSID with client isolation
choices.why: Isolation stops forwarding between guests; it does not stop anybody listening to the air.

prompt: A clinic has 40 staff on WPA2-Personal and a receptionist has just left with the passphrase. The manager wants this never to need a change on 40 devices again. What fixes it?
hint: The problem is that the secret is shared.

choices.text: Moving to WPA3-Personal
choices.why: SAE fixes offline guessing and forward secrecy; the password is still shared by all 40.

choices.text: A longer passphrase, changed every month
choices.why: That is the 40-device change, monthly.

choices.text: 802.1X with one account per person
choices.why: Right. Disabling one account removes one person.

choices.text: Hiding the SSID and filtering by MAC address
choices.why: Neither controls access: the name and the addresses are both on the air in clear.

prompt: psk.py put 8 random lowercase letters at 37.6 bits. How many bits do 16 random lowercase letters give? One decimal place.
hint: Bits add when length doubles.

prompt: A client with protected management frames receives a deauthentication frame carrying its AP's address but no valid signature. What does it do?
hint: That frame is what 802.11w signs.

choices.text: Disconnects, then reconnects with a fresh handshake
choices.why: That is what a client without PMF does, and why PMF exists.

choices.text: Ignores it and stays associated
choices.why: Right. A frame it cannot verify is not obeyed.

choices.text: Switches the network to transition mode
choices.why: Clients do not change a network's security mode; the AP's configuration does.

choices.text: Reports it to the RADIUS server
choices.why: PMF works the same on Personal networks with no RADIUS server at all.

prompt: In the hostapd.conf example, the line that stops two guests on the same AP from reaching each other is `___=1`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.
